OpenSkyLab · interactive UAV

Image metadata reader

Check your photos and flight logs together. Traceable matching, a metadata check and a report — with no data upload.

Drop a drone image, a multispectral band, a GeoTIFF orthomosaic or a video, and the reader lists all the metadata it finds in the file: EXIF, XMP, MakerNotes, ICC, IPTC and the file structure itself. It then compares them with the OpenSkyLab metadata specification and shows what the image can supply and what must come from the flight log, the calibration or the field. Files are read only in your browser; nothing is uploaded.

Why it matters

Drone data are only as reusable as their description. What is needed to process and reuse a survey is split between the images, the flight and GNSS logs, the calibration and the field notes. General tools list the tags of one file. They do not join an image with its exposure in the log, do not check what decides the quality of photogrammetry (RTK state, timing, base coverage, overlap), and do not say which fields of a metadata standard are still missing. This reader does that for a whole flight, in your browser, against the open OpenSkyLab specification, and writes files that processing software and data repositories can take directly.

What sets this reader apart

  • Reads flight and GNSS logsDJI MRK, RINEX, SBF, ULog, ArduPilot, eBee, Wingtra and more, which general metadata tools do not read, and matches them with the images.
  • Checks what matters for mappingRTK state and σ of every exposure, camera clock against GNSS, base coverage, overlap, motion blur.
  • Fills the OpenSkyLab metadataShows for every field whether it comes from the image, the log, or is missing. Exports metadata.json, image_log.csv, camera positions and a flight report.
  • Nothing to install, nothing uploadedEverything runs in your browser. ExifTool lists the tags of any file; this reader is built for drone surveys.

Reading results

Details:

Files

Images

or drop them here. JPEG, TIFF, DNG, GeoTIFF, PNG, WebP, HEIC, MP4/MOV, CR2/NEF/ARW; several files at once are fine.

Flight log and GNSS (optional)

DJI Timestamp.MRK, RINEX (also .crx, .gz), RTCM, Septentrio SBF, PX4 ULog, ArduPilot .bin/.log/.tlog, NMEA, GPX, KML, senseFly eBee .bb3, Wingtra, CSV geotags. Adds the exact exposure positions, σ, RTK state and time. Files are recognised by their content, so either box will do.

Your file stays with you. It is read in the browser's memory; the page sends and stores nothing. The one exception is weather from Open-Meteo: only when you ask for it, the approximate position and date of the flight are sent. Note that a phone photo usually carries the exact position and the device serial number.

Try a sample

The samples are synthetic files made for teaching (values are illustrative, not real measurements).

    Tasks

    1 · RTK and ground control

    Load sample 1. Find the GNSS solution state, the RtkFlag value and the position standard deviations. How many ground control points would you plan for such a flight, and what would check points still be good for? Explain.

    2 · Three heights of one image

    For sample 4 compare GPSAltitude from EXIF with AbsoluteAltitude and RelativeAltitude from XMP drone-dji. Explain which surface each refers to and which one goes into the alt_ellipsoid_m column. What must you check about your drone model?

    3 · What your phone gives away

    Take any outdoor photo with your phone and load it (it is not uploaded). Open the list of what to remove before sharing. Which items identify you, and why must you not delete them from photogrammetric data? Also find the photo's time zone: why does sample 1 lack one, and what does that mean for the UTC time and the sun position?

    4 · GSD against the flight planner

    For sample 1 set the flight height so that the GSD comes out at 2.5 cm/px and compare it with your flight planner. Why does the computed GSD hold only for flat ground at the take-off elevation, and how does it change over a slope or a tree canopy?

    5 · A multispectral band

    Load samples 3 and 4 and find the band, its wavelength and the irradiance from the sun sensor. Why is the MicaSense value converted to µW·cm⁻²·nm⁻¹ while the DJI value stays without a unit? What follows for the irradiance_dls column?

    6 · What an image never tells

    In the OpenSkyLab check choose the Core profile and list the fields that no image can fill. For each, say where the value comes from and explain why the specification still requires it.

    7 · Checking a batch

    Load the sample flight (8 images) and find the images that differ from the rest in the Batch view. Decide which you would exclude from photogrammetric processing or process separately, and explain why.

    8 · Content provenance (C2PA)

    Load sample 6 and find in the Overview who created the record, which actions it lists and which digital source type it states. Why does the reader report “no signature”, and why can you not trust such a record? What must a verifier check for a signed manifest, and what happens to Content Credentials when you strip the metadata before sharing?

    What the reader does and does not do

    The reader is a standalone JavaScript parser (OSLMeta 1.0) that reads the file's bytes directly in the browser; the same code is available as a module for the image-upload app. It walks all JPEG segments, TIFF/BigTIFF/DNG directories including sub-directories, GeoTIFF keys, XMP (including Extended XMP), ICC profiles, IPTC IIM, PNG and WebP chunks and the main HEIC/MP4 boxes. Tag names and enumerations follow the ExifTool tables; an unknown numeric tag is shown as “Tag 0xABCD” with its raw value. It is not ExifTool: it decodes MakerNotes only for DJI (other vendors are just recognised), does not convert thermal R-JPEG data to temperatures (use the vendor SDK), only reports video telemetry (djmd, dbgi, SRT), and for RAW formats reads only the TIFF directories.

    Model and simplifications. The Derived group holds calculations, not tags from the file. Pixel pitch comes from FocalPlaneXResolution, from DJI CalibratedFocalLength, or is estimated from the 35 mm equivalent (sensor width = 36 mm / crop). GSD = p·H/f and the footprint assume a nadir image over flat ground at the take-off elevation. UTC is taken, in this order, from UTCAtExposure, OffsetTimeOriginal, XMP with a time zone, GNSS time, the MicaSense convention (UTC) and QuickTime CreateDate; a zone from local minus GNSS time is rounded to 15 minutes. The sun position uses the NOAA (Meeus) algorithm with mean refraction. JPEG quality is an IJG-scaling estimate and only indicative for tables of other origin. AbsoluteAltitude is ellipsoidal or above sea level depending on the DJI model, and EXIF GPSAltitude varies between vendors; the reader shows them separately and does not convert between ellipsoid and geoid. The check against the OpenSkyLab specification v0.3 uses the reader's own rules; image_log.csv and metadata.json are drafts to complete and review. The samples are synthetic and for teaching only.

    Flight logs and geometry. Logs are read by a separate module (OSLFlight) and matched with the images by file name, DJI MRK index, CaptureId or time. When an image is matched, the OpenSkyLab check takes the exposure time, position, RTK state and σ from the log (the height only when the log gives it above the ellipsoid) and shows the image's own value next to it for comparison: positions agree within 1 m, heights within 1 m, times within 0.5 s. The flight geometry (lines, spacing, overlap, motion blur) is computed from the exposure positions in the log, or from the image positions without a log, with the camera footprint for flat ground at take-off elevation. From an encrypted DJI FlightRecord v13+ the browser reads only the summary (aircraft, serial numbers, start, duration, photo count); the track and exposures need conversion to CSV with dji-log-parser first.

    Content Credentials (C2PA). The reader finds C2PA manifest stores in JPEG (APP11 JPEG XT segments, reassembled by box instance and sequence number), PNG (caBX chunk), TIFF (tag 0xCD41), WebP (C2PA chunk) and ISO BMFF (uuid box). It walks the JUMBF boxes, decodes the CBOR claim and assertions, and from the COSE_Sign1 signature it lists the algorithm and the names in the signer's certificate; the active manifest is the last one in the store, and the digital source type is explained with the IPTC vocabulary. It does not verify the signature, the certificate chain, the time stamp or the content hashes; use the official verifier or the c2pa library for that. Sample 6 carries a deliberately unsigned manifest.

    What the individual drone tags mean is explained by the lab What is inside a drone image; the metadata specification is described on the Metadata pages.
